 7.Since the orders under challenge before us were passed in an appeal  arising out of a trial under the Collaborators Order, let us first examine the text  of article 16 thereof which deals with the topic of appeals. It will be observed that while by clause (1) and the first part of clause (2) of article 16 provision has been made in the Collaborators Order for appeals to the High Court Division respectively against orders of conviction and acquittal, clause (3) simply prescribes the period of limitation for such appeals and clause (4) says that appeals may lie on matters of fact as well as of law. Clause (5) conferred on the Government a right to move the High Court Division for revision of sentences passed by Special Tribunals and Special Magistrates in respect of certain offences punishable under the Collaborators Order within a specified period, which has since expired. The second part of clause (2) of this article, which needs special mention, provides that in a case ending in acquittal, upon intimation to the Special Tribunal or the Special Magistrate, as the case may be, that an appeal is being filed against the order of acquittal the person in respect of whom the order of acquittal is passed "shall continue to remain in custody". 

 18. The second part of clause (2) of article 16 thus provides legal protection to the 'continuance' in custody of an acquitted accused which would otherwise be unquestionably illegal, upon fulfillment of the condition specified therein. This clause of article 16 has provided a period of limitation of 60 days for preferring an appeal against an order of acquittal. It has not, however, specified a time limit to the continuance of such custody nor does it say that such custody shall continue even after the High Court Division comes to be in   seisin of the appeal. 

 All this leads us inevitably to the conclusion that the protection afforded to the custody of an acquitted accused by the second part of clause (2) of article 16 is intended to extend only upto the point of time when the High Court Division comes to be in seisin of the appeal against the order of acquittal or when the period of limitation for preferring such an appeal expires, whichever is reached earlier. A contrary view would lead to an absurd situation. The proposed appeal against the order of acquittal may not ultimately be filed, or due to some reason or other the appeal may get time-barred. In such a case there would be no authority competent ever to put an end to such custody.
